items.name: StdinMode
items.docs:
Where the child's standard input comes from.

- `Inherit`: the parent's standard input.
- `Null`: an input that is already at its end.
- `Bytes(bytes)`: the given bytes, after which the input ends.
- `Pipe`: a pipe written with [Child.write_bytes!] and ended with
  [Child.close_stdin!]. Only [spawn!] returns a [Child], so with [call!],
  [capture!] and [run!] it means `Null`.
items.head: StdinMode

items.name: StdoutMode
items.signature: [Inherit, InheritStderr, Null, Capture, Tee, Pipe, File(Path, File.WriteMode, File.WriterOptions)]
items.docs:
Where the child's standard output goes.

- `Inherit`: the parent's standard output.
- `InheritStderr`: the parent's standard error, without capturing it.
- `Null`: discarded.
- `Capture`: kept in memory and returned in the [Output].
- `Tee`: captured and also forwarded to the parent's standard output. The
  child sees a pipe, not a terminal.
- `File(path, mode, options)`: open a file once and write directly to it.
  `MergeWithStdout` shares the same open file, including its append mode.
- `Pipe`: queued as chunks for [Child.read!]. Only [spawn!] returns a
  [Child], so with [call!], [capture!] and [run!] it means `Capture`.
items.head: StdoutMode

items.name: StderrMode
items.signature: [Inherit, Null, Capture, Tee, Pipe, File(Path, File.WriteMode, File.WriterOptions), MergeWithStdout]
items.docs:
Where the child's standard error goes: the modes of [StdoutMode], or
`MergeWithStdout`, which sends it into the same OS pipe as standard output.
That keeps the order in which the child wrote to the two streams, which two
separate streams cannot. The merged stream follows the standard output
mode and is reported as standard output.
items.head: StderrMode

items.name: ExitStatus
items.docs:
How a child ended: `Exited(code)` with its exit code, or `Signaled(signal)`
when a signal terminated it. `Signaled` is reported on Unix only.
items.head: ExitStatus

items.name: PartialOutput
items.docs: The output captured before a deadline or an output limit stopped a command.
items.head: PartialOutput

items.name: new
items.docs:
Create a new command with the given program name. Execute it with
[call!], [capture!], [run!] or [spawn!].

```roc
cmd = Cmd.new("ls")
```

The program is an [OsStr]. A string literal can be passed directly, and so
can a literal that interpolates: `Cmd.new("${tool}")`.

items.name: call!
items.docs: Run a command with inherited standard streams and require success.

items.name: capture!
items.signature: OsStr, List(OsStr) => Try(Str, [CmdErr(Err), BadExitStatus(Output), BadUtf8({ problem : Str.Utf8Problem, index : U64 }), Interrupted])
items.docs: Run a command successfully and return its standard output as text.

items.name: run!
items.docs: Run a command and return its captured output and exit status.

items.name: spawn!
items.docs: Start a command with inherited standard streams without waiting.

items.name: exec!
items.docs:
Replace this Unix process with an executable at an exact pathname.

Success never returns and preserves the process ID. The path is relative
to the current directory or absolute; there is no PATH search or implicit
shell. Arguments, environment, working directory and standard streams
keep their native meanings. Arguments do not include the program name.

This bypasses Roc cleanup: finish buffered writers, transactions, terminal
raw mode and children beforehand when their cleanup matters. Host-owned
close-on-exec descriptors close, and other child processes remain alive.
A pending caught signal prevents replacement. A returned error leaves the
running Roc application available to handle it.

items.name: Command
items.signature:
{
		args : List(OsStr),
		clear_envs : Bool,
		envs : List((OsStr, OsStr)),
		program : OsStr,
		cwd_value : [Inherit, Dir(Path)],
		stdin_value : [Unset, Set([Inherit, Null, Bytes(List(U8)), Pipe])],
		stdout_value : [Unset, Set(StdoutMode)],
		stderr_value : [Unset, Set(StderrMode)],
		timeout_value : [NoTimeout, After(Duration)],
		output_limit_value : [NoLimit, MaxBytes(U64)],
		pending_limit_value : U64,
		manage_tree_value : Bool,
	}
items.docs: A reusable command configuration.
items.head: Command

items.name: arg
items.docs:
Add a single argument to the command.
❗ Shell features like variable substitution (e.g. `$FOO`), glob patterns (e.g. `*.txt`), ... are not available.

```roc
cmd = Cmd.new("ls").arg("-l")
```

items.name: args
items.docs:
Add multiple arguments to the command.
❗ Shell features like variable substitution (e.g. `$FOO`), glob patterns (e.g. `*.txt`), ... are not available.

```roc
cmd = Cmd.new("ls").args(["-l", "-a"])
```

For a `List(Str)` use `cmd.args(names.map(OsStr.from_str))`.

items.name: env
items.docs:
Add a single environment variable to the command.

```roc
cmd = Cmd.new("env").env("FOO", "bar") # add the environment variable "FOO" with value "bar"
```

items.name: envs
items.docs:
Add multiple environment variables to the command.

```roc
cmd = Cmd.new("env").envs([("FOO", "bar"), ("BAZ", "qux")])
```

items.name: clear_envs
items.docs:
Clear all environment variables before running the command.
Only environment variables added via `env` or `envs` will be available.
Useful if you want a clean command run that does not behave unexpectedly if the user has some env var set.

```roc
cmd =
    Cmd.new("env")
        .clear_envs()
        .env("ONLY_THIS", "visible")
```

items.name: cwd
items.docs:
Set the child working directory without changing the parent directory.
Use an absolute executable path or a bare PATH name: resolving a relative
executable against cwd is platform-specific.

items.name: stdin
items.docs:
Choose the child's standard input; see [StdinMode].

When this is not called, [run!] gives the child `Null`, and [call!],
[capture!] and [spawn!] let it inherit the parent's standard input.

items.name: stdout
items.docs:
Choose where the child's standard output goes; see [StdoutMode].

When this is not called, [run!] and [capture!] capture it, and [call!] and
[spawn!] let it go to the parent's standard output.

items.name: stderr
items.docs:
Choose where the child's standard error goes; see [StderrMode].

When this is not called, [run!] captures it, and [call!], [capture!] and
[spawn!] let it go to the parent's standard error.

items.name: inherit_stdio
items.docs:
Let the child use the parent's standard input, output and error, however
the command is run. With [run!] this gives the exit status of a command
that prints to the terminal:

```roc
status = Cmd.new("roc").args(["check", "main.roc"]).inherit_stdio().run!()?.status
```

items.name: timeout
items.docs:
Stop the command when it has run for longer than `duration`. The deadline
covers the whole run, including reading the rest of its output.

A command that reaches its deadline is killed, and the result is
`Err(CmdErr(TimedOut(partial)))` with the output captured so far. That is
also what [Child.wait!] and [Child.poll!] return for a child started with
[spawn!]. When `timeout` is not called there is no deadline;
`Duration.zero` expires immediately.

items.name: output_limit
items.docs:
Limit how many bytes of standard output and standard error are captured,
counted together. The default is `MaxBytes(16777216)`, 16 MiB.

A command that prints more is killed, and the result is
`Err(CmdErr(OutputLimitExceeded(partial)))` with the output captured up to
the limit. `NoLimit` captures whatever the command prints.

items.name: pending_limit
items.docs:
Limit how many bytes of `Pipe` output may wait to be read with
[Child.read!], counted over both streams (default 1 MiB). A child that
gets further ahead of its reader is killed, and [Child.wait!] returns
`Err(CmdErr(OutputLimitExceeded(partial)))`.

items.name: manage_tree
items.docs:
Also terminate descendants on cancellation, using a Unix process group
or Windows Job Object. Disabled by default; descendants must not escape it.

items.name: call!
items.docs:
Run the command on the parent's terminal and require it to succeed.

Standard input, output and error are inherited unless the command sets
them. Any status other than exit code 0 is `Err(BadExitStatus(output))`.

```roc
Cmd.new("cargo").args(["build", "--release"]).call!()?
```

items.name: capture!
items.signature: Command => Try(Str, [CmdErr(Err), BadExitStatus(Output), BadUtf8({ problem : Str.Utf8Problem, index : U64 }), Interrupted])
items.docs:
Run the command, require it to succeed, and return its standard output as
text.

Standard output is captured unless the command sets it. Standard input and
standard error are inherited unless the command sets them, so warnings
still reach the terminal, as with a shell's `$(..)`. Any status other than
exit code 0 is `Err(BadExitStatus(output))`, and output that is not UTF-8
is `Err(BadUtf8(..))`.

The text is returned as printed, including a final newline:

```roc
sha = Cmd.new("git").args(["rev-parse", "${branch}"]).capture!()?.trim()
```

items.name: run!
items.docs:
Run the command and return its exit status and output as data. A non-zero
exit code or a signal is not an error here: match on `output.status`, or
call [Output.require_success].

Standard output and standard error are captured, and standard input is
`Null`, unless the command sets them. The result is returned once the
command has exited and all of its output has been read.

```roc
output = Cmd.new("roc").args(["check", "main.roc"]).run!()?
```

items.name: spawn!
items.docs:
Start the command and return a [Child] without waiting for it.

Standard input, output and error are inherited unless the command sets
them. Set a stream to `Pipe` to exchange data with the child while it runs.
Keep the returned child for later reads, waits or cleanup; an unused
binding such as `_child` does not keep the process alive. See [Child].

items.name: to_str
items.docs:
The program and its arguments, separated by spaces, for messages and logs.
An argument that is empty or contains a space or a quote is written as a
quoted, escaped string. The environment, the working directory and the
other settings are not included.

```roc
expect Cmd.new("git").args(["commit", "-m", "first draft"]).to_str() == "git commit -m \"first draft\""
```

items.name: to_inspect
items.docs:
Customize command output for `Str.inspect`: the full configuration, with
the names of the environment variables it sets but never their values, and
the length of `Bytes` input but not its content.

items.name: check_available!
items.docs:
Report whether `command` can be found on the system as something runnable.

A bare name (like `"git"`) is looked up across the `PATH` entries; a name
containing a path separator is checked as-is. On Windows the candidate
extensions come from `%PATHEXT%`.

On Unix this checks for an executable bit; a directory is not reported even
though it carries one, though a symbolic link to a directory is a rare
exception.

items.name: Err
items.docs:
Why a command could not be started or did not run to completion. A
non-zero exit code is not one of these: it is `BadExitStatus`, or the
`status` of an [Output].

- `StartFailed(err, program)`: the program could not be started, for
  example `StartFailed(NotFound, program)` when it does not exist.
- `TimedOut(partial)`: the command reached the deadline set with
  [Command.timeout] and was killed.
- `OutputLimitExceeded(partial)`: the command printed more than
  [Command.output_limit] or [Command.pending_limit] allows and was killed.
- `IOErr(err)`: an operating-system failure while the command ran. A
  [Child.read!] or [Child.write_bytes!] that waited for its whole
  `Duration` is `IOErr(TimedOut)`.
items.head: Err

items.name: is_eq
items.docs: Compare two errors, so results that contain one work with `==`.

items.name: to_str
items.docs: Describe the error in a sentence, without the captured output.

items.name: to_inspect
items.docs:
Customize error output for `Str.inspect`. Captured output is shown as
text, with invalid UTF-8 replaced, not as a list of bytes.

items.name: Output
items.signature: { command : Str, status : ExitStatus, stdout_bytes : List(U8), stderr_bytes : List(U8) }
items.docs:
The result of a command that ran to completion: how it ended and what it
printed. `command` is the program and arguments, as [Command.to_str] renders them.
Output is empty for a stream that was not captured.
items.head: Output

items.name: is_eq
items.docs: Compare two outputs, so results that contain one work with `==`.

items.name: require_success
items.docs:
Turn any status other than exit code 0 into `Err(BadExitStatus(output))`.

```roc
bytes = cmd.run!()?.require_success()?.stdout_bytes
```

items.name: stdout_utf8
items.signature: Output -> Try(Str, [BadUtf8({ problem : Str.Utf8Problem, index : U64 })])
items.docs:
The captured standard output as text, or `BadUtf8` when it is not
valid UTF-8.

items.name: stdout_utf8_lossy
items.docs:
The captured standard output as text, with invalid UTF-8 replaced by
the Unicode replacement character.

items.name: stderr_utf8_lossy
items.docs:
The captured standard error as text, with invalid UTF-8 replaced by
the Unicode replacement character.

items.name: to_inspect
items.docs:
Customize output for `Str.inspect`. Captured output is shown as text,
with invalid UTF-8 replaced, not as a list of bytes.

items.name: Child
items.signature: { host : Resource.Child, pid_value : U32, command : Str, program : OsStr }
items.docs:
A running command started with [spawn!].

When the last reference to a child is released, a child that is still
running is killed and reaped. Use [Child.close!] to do that at a chosen
point. After `close!` every other operation returns `Err(Closed)`.
An unused binding, including `_child`, can release the last reference
immediately. Keep a reference that a later read, wait or cleanup uses.
items.head: Child

items.name: pid
items.docs: The operating-system process identifier the child was started with.

items.name: wait!
items.docs:
Wait for the child to exit and for all of its output to be read, then
return its status and captured output. A piped standard input is
closed first, so exchange data with [write_bytes!] and [read!] before
waiting. Waiting again returns the same result.

`Pipe` output is available only through [read!]; its output field in
this result is empty. Choose `Capture` to retain that stream for
`wait!`, subject to the command's [Command.output_limit].

items.name: poll!
items.docs:
Check on the child without waiting: `Running`, or `Finished(output)`
once it has exited and all of its output has been read.

items.name: kill!
items.docs:
Ask the operating system to kill the child. This does not wait: use
[wait!] to see it end. Killing a child that has exited does nothing.

items.name: close_stdin!
items.docs:
Close a piped standard input so the child sees the end of its input.
Closing it again does nothing.

items.name: close!
items.docs:
Kill a child that is still running, reap it, and close the handle for
every reference to it. Closing again does nothing.

items.name: read!
items.signature: Child, Duration => Try([Stdout(List(U8)), Stderr(List(U8))], [EndOfInput, CmdErr(Cmd.Err), Closed, Interrupted])
items.docs:
Return the next chunk of `Pipe` output, from whichever stream has
one, waiting up to `wait` for it. The host picks the chunk size.

`Duration.zero` does not wait: it returns a chunk that is ready, and
otherwise times out. A wait that expires is
`Err(CmdErr(IOErr(TimedOut)))`; the child keeps running and may be
read again. Once the child has exited and every chunk has been
returned, the result is `Err(EndOfInput)`.

```roc
chunk = child.read!(Duration.seconds(1))?
```

items.name: write_bytes!
items.signature: Child, List(U8), Duration => Try({}, [CmdErr(Cmd.Err), Closed, Interrupted])
items.docs:
Write bytes to a piped standard input, waiting up to `wait` for the
child to accept all of them. `Duration.zero` makes one attempt that
does not wait.

A wait that expires is `Err(CmdErr(IOErr(TimedOut)))`. Part of the
input may have been delivered by then, or before `Interrupted`, so writing all of it again can
duplicate bytes. Writing when standard input is not a pipe, or after
[close_stdin!], is `Err(CmdErr(IOErr(BrokenPipe)))`.

items.name: write_utf8!
items.signature: Child, Str, Duration => Try({}, [CmdErr(Cmd.Err), Closed, Interrupted])
items.docs: Write text to a piped standard input as UTF-8; see [write_bytes!].

items.name: Duration
items.docs:
A non-negative length of time with nanosecond resolution.

Build one from a unit, `Duration.seconds(5)`, and pass it wherever a timeout
or a wait is expected. Durations support `+`, `-`, `==` and the ordering
operators, and sort with `List.sort`.

Every result is clamped to what a `Duration` can hold: zero at the low end
and [U64.highest] nanoseconds (about 584 years) at the high end. Nothing here
crashes on overflow, so `a - b` is [Duration.zero] when `b` is longer than `a`.
items.head: Duration

items.name: zero
items.docs: The empty duration. A timeout of `Duration.zero` expires immediately.

items.name: nanos
items.docs: A duration of the given number of nanoseconds.

items.name: millis
items.docs:
A duration of the given number of milliseconds, clamped to the longest
representable duration.

items.name: seconds
items.docs:
A duration of the given number of seconds, clamped to the longest
representable duration.

items.name: minutes
items.docs:
A duration of the given number of minutes, clamped to the longest
representable duration.

items.name: to_nanos
items.docs: The length of this duration in nanoseconds.

items.name: to_millis
items.docs:
The length of this duration in whole milliseconds, truncating any
remainder: 1999 microseconds is 1 millisecond.

items.name: to_seconds
items.docs: The length of this duration in whole seconds, truncating any remainder.

items.name: to_str
items.docs:
Format this duration for people, in the largest unit that fits:
nanoseconds below a millisecond (`"999ns"`), whole milliseconds below a
second (`"250ms"`), then seconds with up to three decimals (`"1.5s"`,
`"10800s"`). Digits past the unit's precision are truncated, not rounded.

items.name: to_inspect
items.docs: How `Str.inspect` renders a duration: `Duration(1.5s)`.

items.name: sleep!
items.docs:
Pause the current process for this duration.

Use this for a wait that was computed, such as
`interval.minus(start.elapsed!()).sleep!()`; `Sleep.millis!(250)` reads
better for a literal one. `Duration.zero` returns immediately.

items.name: plus
items.docs: Add two durations (`a + b`), clamped to the longest representable duration.

items.name: minus
items.docs:
Subtract one duration from another (`a - b`), giving [Duration.zero] when
`b` is the longer one.

This gives several timed operations one budget:
`budget - start.elapsed!()` is the time left, and is zero once the budget
is spent.

items.name: is_eq
items.docs: Compare two durations for equality (`==` and `!=`).

items.name: is_lt
items.docs: Whether the first duration is shorter than the second (`<`).

items.name: is_lte
items.docs: Whether the first duration is no longer than the second (`<=`).

items.name: is_gt
items.docs: Whether the first duration is longer than the second (`>`).

items.name: is_gte
items.docs: Whether the first duration is at least as long as the second (`>=`).

items.name: order_relative_to
items.docs:
Order two durations, shortest first. This is what `List.sort` and
`List.sort_by` use.

items.name: dict!
items.docs:
Return all environment variables as native name/value pairs.

Native non-Unicode values are preserved. Iteration order is unspecified
and may differ between calls or operating systems.

items.name: var!
items.docs:
Reads the given environment variable.

Returns `Err(VarNotFound(name))` if the variable is not set.

items.name: var_str!
items.docs: Reads the given environment variable as a string if its native value is valid text.

items.name: cwd!
items.docs:
Reads the [current working directory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_directory)
from the environment.

Returns `Err(CwdUnavailable)` if the cwd cannot be determined.

items.name: set_cwd!
items.docs:
Change the process current working directory.

Returns `Err(InvalidCwd(err))` when the path cannot be used as a working
directory. The process-wide change remains in effect until changed again.

items.name: exe_path!
items.docs:
Gets the path to the currently-running executable.

Returns `Err(ExePathUnavailable)` if the path cannot be determined.

items.name: program_name!
items.docs:
Gets the program name supplied by the process launcher as its first argument.

This is conventionally the executable name or path, but launchers may supply
another value. Unlike [`exe_path!`](#exe_path!), it is returned as an
[`OsStr`](OsStr), preserving the value exactly without treating it as a path.
Returns `Err(ProgramNameUnavailable)` if the launcher supplied no first argument.

items.name: create_temp_dir!
items.docs:
Atomically create a private directory in the system temporary directory.
The caller owns cleanup. Unix directories have mode 0700.

items.name: create_temp_dir_with_prefix!
items.docs: Create a private temporary directory with a filename prefix.

items.name: create_temp_dir_in!
items.docs:
Create a private temporary directory under an existing parent directory.
Prefixes cannot contain separators, colons, NUL, or be `.` or `..`.

items.name: with_temp_dir!
items.signature: (Path.Path => Try(a, err)) => Try(a, [TempDirErr(IOErr), CallbackErr(err), CleanupErr(IOErr, Path.Path), CallbackAndCleanupErr(err, IOErr, Path.Path)])
items.docs:
Run a callback with a private directory and delete the directory afterward.
Cleanup is attempted after callback success and failure. If both fail, both errors are returned.

```roc
Env.with_temp_dir!(|directory| {
	file = Path.join(directory, "result.txt")
	Path.write_utf8!(file, "temporary data")?
	Path.read_utf8!(file)
})?
```

items.name: temp_dir!
items.docs: Gets the default directory for temporary files.

items.name: SeekFrom
items.docs: A byte offset from the start, current logical position, or end of a file.
items.head: SeekFrom

items.name: Reader
items.docs:
A buffered file reader.

The file is closed when the last reference to the reader is released.
Copies of a reader share one cursor and one buffer, so every read,
whether of lines, delimited bytes or binary data, continues where the
previous one stopped.

Every read ends the same way: once all data has been returned, the next
read is `Err(EndOfInput)`. An empty `Ok` is real data, such as an empty
line. A read may be repeated after `EndOfInput`; if the file has grown
it returns the new data.
items.head: Reader

items.name: to_inspect
items.docs: Render the reader without exposing its host handle.

items.name: read_up_to!
items.docs:
Read at most `max_bytes` bytes. Short reads are valid, even before
the end of the file. Asking for zero bytes performs no I/O and
returns `Ok([])`; otherwise the result is never empty, and the end
of the file is `Err(EndOfInput)`.
Returned bytes remain valid after later reads or seeks.

items.name: read_exactly!
items.docs:
Read exactly `count` bytes, or report `UnexpectedEndOfInput`.
Zero succeeds without I/O. Errors may consume bytes; partial data is
not returned and the cursor is not restored.

items.name: read_until!
items.docs:
Read bytes through and including the next `delimiter`.

If the file ends first, the bytes before the end are returned without
a delimiter, and the read after that is `Err(EndOfInput)`. So the
result is never empty, and its last byte shows whether the delimiter
arrived: to follow a growing file line by line, use
`reader.read_until!('\n')` rather than [read_line!].

items.name: read_line!
items.signature: Reader => Try(Str, [EndOfInput, BadUtf8({ problem : Str.Utf8Problem, index : U64 }), FileErr(IOErr)])
items.docs:
Read a line of text.

A line ends at `\n`. The terminator is not returned, and one `\r`
before it is removed. A file that ends without a `\n` still yields
its last line; after that the result is `Err(EndOfInput)`. An empty
line is `Ok("")`. Lines have no length limit.

A line that is not valid UTF-8 is consumed and reported as `BadUtf8`;
the next call reads the line after it. For the bytes of a line, use
`reader.read_until!('\n')`.

items.name: position!
items.docs: Return the byte position of the next read, accounting for buffered bytes.

items.name: seek!
items.docs:
Move the shared cursor and return its new absolute byte position.
Seeking past EOF does not extend the file. Invalid offsets and sources
that cannot seek report FileErr. A failed seek need not restore the cursor.
Aliases of this reader observe the same cursor.

items.name: lines
items.signature: Reader -> Stream(Try(Str, [BadUtf8({ problem : Str.Utf8Problem, index : U64 }), FileErr(IOErr)]))

items.name: chunks
items.docs:
Lazily read this reader as non-empty chunks of at most 64 KiB.
Chunk boundaries do not correspond to records, newlines, or text
encoding boundaries. For a chosen size, call [read_up_to!] in a loop.

Building the stream reads nothing; each item is one read from the
shared cursor. The stream ends at the end of the file. A `FileErr`
item is the last one; the reader stays usable and a new stream may be
started, for example after a [seek!]. Retained chunks remain valid.

```roc
for! item in reader.chunks() {
    bytes = item?
    $total = $total + bytes.len()
}
```

The stream keeps the file open until it has finished or is released.
Process chunks individually to bound memory; `Stream.collect!`
accumulates every chunk.

items.name: WriteMode
items.docs:
What opening a [Writer] does to the file at the path.

- `Truncate` creates the file, or empties it if it exists.
- `Append` creates the file if it is missing and keeps what it holds;
  every write goes to the end.
- `RequireNew` creates the file and fails with `AlreadyExists` if
  anything is at the path.
items.head: WriteMode

items.name: WriterOptions
items.docs:
Explicit access policies apply only when a regular file is newly created.
OwnerOnly grants the owner read/write and others no access; PublicRead
additionally grants everyone read. Both replace inherited ACL grants.
Existing files keep their permissions. Use RequireNew with OwnerOnly for
secrets. Filesystems that cannot enforce a policy return Unsupported.
items.head: WriterOptions

items.name: Writer
items.docs:
A buffered file writer.

Written bytes are held in a buffer in the host and reach the operating
system when the buffer fills and on [flush!]. A write accepts all of
its bytes or fails. Copies of a writer share one file and one buffer.

There is no `close!`: the file is closed when the last reference to the
writer is released. Bytes still buffered then are written, but a
failure to write them cannot be reported, so call [flush!] after the
last write, or use [File.with_writer!], which does it for you.

items.name: write_stream!
items.docs:
Write each chunk of a stream as it arrives, holding one chunk in
memory at a time.

Stops at the first `Err` item, which is returned as `SourceErr`; the
chunks before it have been written. A failed write is `FileErr`.
Nothing is flushed at the end.

Any stream of byte chunks will do: `reader.chunks()`,
`Stdin.chunks()`, the `response.chunks()` of an
[Http.send_streaming!](Http.send_streaming!) response, or a stream
mapped from one of them.

```roc
reader = File.open_reader!(source)?
File.with_writer!(destination, Truncate, {}, |writer|
    writer.write_stream!(reader.chunks().map(|chunk| chunk.map_ok(redact))))?
```

items.docs:
Hand every buffered byte to the operating system.

This is the call that reports whether the bytes written so far
reached the file. It does not force them to the storage device.

items.name: open_reader!
items.docs:

Failing to open reports the path, using the same `PathErr` as the
whole-file operations so both combine in one error type.

```roc

first_line = reader.read_line!()?
```

items.name: open_writer!
items.docs:
Open a file for buffered writing. The [WriteMode] decides whether
existing data survives, so it has no default.

Failing to open reports the path, as [File.open_reader!] does.

Prefer [File.with_writer!]: with a writer opened here, a `?` on a write
returns before the final [flush!](File.Writer.flush!), and the failure
of the flush that happens on release is not reported.

```roc

log.write_utf8!("started\n")?
log.flush!()?
```

items.name: StreamingOptions
items.docs:
Options for [Http.send_streaming!]. `{}` selects the defaults.

`idle_timeout` bounds each single wait: for the status and headers, and
then for each part of the body. A server that is silent for that long
has stalled, however much it has already sent. It defaults to 30
seconds; `After(Duration.zero)` expires at once, before anything is
sent, and `NoTimeout` waits for as long as the server takes.

The timeout of the `Request` keeps its meaning: it is the deadline for
the whole exchange, body included, and `NoTimeout` (its default) and
`TimeoutMilliseconds(0)` both mean no deadline. For a large download
leave the request at `NoTimeout` and rely on `idle_timeout`.

`max_redirects` has the same meaning as the `max_redirects` field of [SendOptions].
A caught pending signal returns bare `Interrupted` from a wait. Body
reads preserve their cursor and collected bytes after interruption;
acknowledge the signal before reading again. The deadline keeps running.
items.head: StreamingOptions

items.name: send_streaming!
items.docs:
Validate and send an HTTP request, returning once the status and
headers have arrived. The body is read afterwards, through the
[StreamingResponse].

The request is validated, built and sent exactly as [Http.send!] does
it. Any status is `Ok`, so check it before reading the body. Either
timeout expiring is `Err(HttpErr(Timeout))`.

```roc
request = Request.from_method(GET).with_uri(url.to_str())
response = Http.send_streaming!(request, {})?
if response.status() != 200 {
    return Err(UnexpectedStatus(response.status()))
}
File.with_writer!(destination, Truncate, {}, |writer| writer.write_stream!(response.chunks()))?
```

items.name: StreamingResponse
items.docs:
The status and headers of a response, and its body still to be read.

The body arrives over the response's own connection as it is read.
[StreamingResponse.chunks] and [read_to_end!] read from one shared
cursor, as do copies of the response, so each byte of the body is
returned once.

The connection is closed when the body ends, when a failure other than
an idle timeout ends it, or when the last reference to the response and
its streams is released; a body that is not wanted need not be read.
items.head: StreamingResponse

items.name: to_inspect
items.docs: Render the status and headers without exposing the host handle.

items.name: status
items.docs:
The status code. Any status is a response: a 404 is `Ok` with
`status()` 404, and its body can be read or left alone.

items.name: headers
items.docs: The response headers, in the order they arrived.

items.name: content_length
items.docs:
The length of the whole body in bytes, from the `Content-Length`
header. `Unknown` when the server did not send one, as with a
chunked body. For the response to a `HEAD` request this is the
length the header declares, although no body follows.

items.name: chunks
items.docs:
Lazily read the body as non-empty chunks of at most 64 KiB. Chunk
boundaries are chosen by the host and carry no meaning.

Building the stream reads nothing; each item is one read from the
shared cursor. The stream ends at the end of the body, and a
failure is the last item.

After an idle timeout, `Err(HttpErr(Timeout))` with the response's
deadline not yet reached, the response stays usable and a new
`chunks()` continues where the last one stopped. Any other failure
is final: a new stream yields it again.

```roc
response = Http.send_streaming!(request, { idle_timeout: After(Duration.seconds(5)) })?
var $done = 0
for! item in response.chunks() {
    bytes = item?
    $done = $done + bytes.len()
}
```

Process chunks individually to bound memory; `Stream.collect!`
accumulates every chunk.

items.name: read_to_end!
items.docs:
Read the rest of the body: everything [StreamingResponse.chunks]
and earlier reads have not returned. At the end of the body that is
`Ok([])`.

With `MaxBytes(max)` this fails with `ReadLimitExceeded(max)` as
soon as more than `max` unread bytes have arrived, without waiting
for the rest. `NoLimit` holds the whole remainder in memory.

A failed call consumes nothing it could keep: after
`ReadLimitExceeded` or an idle timeout the bytes that had arrived
are still unread, so [StreamingResponse.chunks] or another call
continues from the same place.

```roc
body = response.read_to_end!(MaxBytes(1_048_576))?
```

items.name: IOErr
items.signature:
[
	AddrInUse,
	AddrNotAvailable,
	AlreadyExists,
	BrokenPipe,
	ConnectionRefused,
	ConnectionReset,
	Interrupted,
	IsADirectory,
	NotFound,
	NotADirectory,
	Other(Str),
	OutOfMemory,
	PermissionDenied,
	TimedOut,
	Unsupported,
]
items.docs:
Represents an I/O error that can occur during platform operations.

**NotFound** - An entity was not found, often a file.

**PermissionDenied** - The operation lacked the necessary privileges to complete.

**BrokenPipe** - The operation failed because a pipe was closed.

**AlreadyExists** - An entity already exists, often a file.

**AddrInUse** - A socket address could not be bound because it is already in use.

**AddrNotAvailable** - The requested socket address does not exist or is not local.

**ConnectionRefused** - The remote host refused the connection.

**ConnectionReset** - The remote host reset the connection.

**Interrupted** - This operation was interrupted. Interrupted operations can typically be retried.

**IsADirectory** - A filesystem operation expected a non-directory path.

**NotADirectory** - A filesystem operation expected a directory path.

**Unsupported** - This operation is unsupported on this platform. This means that the operation can never succeed.

**OutOfMemory** - An operation could not be completed, because it failed to allocate enough memory.

**TimedOut** - The operation did not complete within its timeout.

**Other** - A custom error that does not fall under any other I/O error kind.

directly wherever an `OsStr` is expected. The host lowers UTF-8 text to the
active OS representation.

named like the other representation constructors.

items.docs: Build an OS string from a quoted string literal.

items.name: from_interpolation
items.docs: Build a UTF-8 OS string from an interpolated string literal.

items.name: parser_for
items.docs: Parse and encode every OS string representation as a lossless tagged value.

items.name: to_str_try
items.docs: Convert an OS string to a string if its raw representation is valid text.

items.name: to_bytes
items.docs:
Convert an OS string to the bytes that represent it, for writing to a byte
stream such as [Stdout.write_bytes!] or [Stderr.write_bytes!].

UTF-8 text and Unix OS strings return their exact bytes, so non-Unicode Unix
data is preserved. Windows OS strings are UTF-16 code units rather than bytes,
so they are encoded as UTF-8 with unpaired surrogates replaced by U+FFFD;
that conversion is lossy and must not be used for roundtripping.

items.name: display
items.docs:
Convert an OS string to a best-effort display string, replacing invalid text
with U+FFFD. This representation is lossy and must not be used for roundtripping.

items.name: to_inspect
items.docs: Customize debug output for `Str.inspect`.

items.name: is_eq
items.docs:
Compare OS strings by content, whichever representation holds it.

A string literal is stored as UTF-8, while the operating system hands
back native units, so `args.contains("--verbose")` and
`Env.var!("EDITOR")? == "vim"` compare text with native units.

- Two values that are valid Unicode are equal when they are the same text,
  in any mix of UTF-8, Unix bytes and Windows UTF-16.
- Unix bytes that are not valid UTF-8, or UTF-16 with an unpaired
  surrogate, equal only the identical units of the same kind, and never a
  UTF-8 value.

Nothing is normalized: case, Unicode normal forms and path separators
all still distinguish two values.

text in every representation, and anything else as its raw units.

items.docs:

bytes and Windows UTF-16 units are preserved across host effects; use
`display` only when a lossy human-readable representation is appropriate.

Quoted literals create UTF-8 paths, and `join` appends one path component:

```roc
Path.create_all!("config")?
config_file = Path.join("config", "app.json")
Path.write_utf8!(config_file, "{}")?
```

items.docs:

This function does not traverse symbolic links; symbolic links (including
broken ones) return `False`.
Sockets, FIFOs, devices, and other special filesystem objects also return `False`.

items.docs:

This function does not traverse symbolic links; symbolic links (including

items.name: is_sym_link!
items.docs:

This function will not traverse symbolic links - it checks whether the path
itself is a symlink.
Sockets, FIFOs, devices, and other special filesystem objects return `False`.

items.docs: Returns `True` if the path exists on disk.

`IsOther` represents sockets, FIFOs, block and character devices, and any
platform-specific object that is not a regular file, directory, or symbolic
link. On Windows this includes unrecognized reparse-point types.

items.docs: Make a path absolute without requiring it to exist. This does not resolve symlinks.

items.docs: Resolve an existing path, including symbolic links, to its absolute native path.

items.name: set_permissions!
items.docs:
Replace discretionary access grants on a regular-file target, preserving
ownership and contents. Symbolic links are followed. OwnerOnly grants
owner read/write; PublicRead additionally grants everyone read. Neither
grants execute. Existing handles and privileged OS access are unaffected.
On macOS the target must currently be readable to open a handle for
replacing its ACL. On Linux repairing an unreadable file requires
/proc/self/fd.

items.name: symlink!
items.docs:

resolves from the link's parent directory. The declared target kind must
match the eventual target; dangling targets are allowed. Windows requires
Developer Mode or permission to create symbolic links.

Rejects same-file copies (including hard-link aliases) and special files.

items.name: copy_dir!
items.signature: Path, Path => Try({}, [CopyErr({ operation : Str, source : Path, destination : Path, error : IOErr })])
items.docs:
Copy a directory tree into a new destination, following symbolic links.
Missing destination parent directories are created.
Permissions are preserved; timestamps, ownership, ACLs and other metadata are not.
Errors may leave a partial destination. Cycles and overlapping source/destination trees are rejected.

items.name: copy_dir_with!
items.signature: Path, Path, { symlinks : [Follow, Preserve], destination : [RequireNew, Merge] } => Try({}, [CopyErr({ operation : Str, source : Path, destination : Path, error : IOErr })])
items.docs:
Choose whether to preserve links and whether to merge an existing destination tree.
Merge replaces regular files. Existing destination directory symlinks are rejected.

items.name: read_bytes!
items.docs: Read all bytes from a file at this path.

items.name: write_bytes!
items.docs: Write bytes to a file at this path, replacing any existing contents.

items.name: read_utf8!
items.docs: Read a UTF-8 file at this path.

items.name: write_utf8!
items.docs: Write a UTF-8 file at this path, replacing any existing contents.

items.name: append_bytes!
items.docs:
Append bytes to the end of the file at this path, creating the file if it
does not exist. Missing parent directories are not created.

Existing contents are never truncated or overwritten: the file is opened in
append mode, so the operating system places the bytes at the current end of
the file even when other writers are appending to it. The bytes are handed
to the operating system in one write, which keeps appends from concurrent
writers from interleaving in the common case, but this is not guaranteed for
large contents or on network filesystems.

The append is not atomic or durable: a failure mid-write can leave part of
the bytes appended, and nothing is flushed to the storage device before
this returns.

items.name: append_utf8!
items.docs:
Append UTF-8 text to the end of the file at this path, creating the file if
it does not exist. No newline is added.

```roc
Path.append_utf8!("events.log", "started\n")?
```

This has the same creation, concurrency and failure behavior as
[append_bytes!].

items.name: replace_utf8!
items.docs:
Replace every occurrence of `pattern` with `replacement` in the UTF-8 file
at this path.

This reads the whole file, substitutes, and writes it back, so it is not
atomic: a failure mid-write can leave the file partially written, exactly
as a bare [write_utf8!] would.

items.name: delete!
items.docs: Delete a file at this path.

items.name: size_in_bytes!
items.docs: Return the size of the file at this path in bytes.

items.name: is_executable!
items.docs: Check whether the file at this path has any executable bit set.

items.name: is_readable!
items.docs: Check whether the file at this path has a readable owner permission bit set.

items.name: is_writable!
items.docs: Check whether the file at this path has a writable owner permission bit set.

items.name: time_accessed!
items.docs:
Return when the file at this path was last accessed.

Times before 1970 are returned as negative instants, not errors.

items.name: time_modified!
items.docs:
Return when the file at this path was last modified.

Times before 1970 are returned as negative instants, not errors.

```roc
stale = Utc.now!().since(path.time_modified!()?) > Duration.minutes(5)
```

items.name: time_created!
items.docs:
Return when the file at this path was created.

Times before 1970 are returned as negative instants, not errors. Fails
with `Unsupported` where the filesystem does not record a creation time.

items.name: hard_link!
items.docs:
Create a hard link at `link` pointing to `original`.

Errors report `original`, which is what a missing-file failure refers to.
Some failures concern `link` instead, such as `AlreadyExists`.

items.name: rename!
items.docs:
Rename a file from `from` to `to`.

Errors report `from`; a failure may still concern `to`, such as its
parent directory not existing.

items.name: create_dir!
items.docs: Create a directory at this path.

items.name: create_all!
items.docs: Create a directory and any missing parent directories at this path.

items.name: delete_empty!
items.docs: Delete an empty directory at this path.

items.name: delete_all!
items.docs: Delete a directory and all contents at this path.

items.name: list!
items.docs:
List the entries in the directory at this path.

The result is all-or-nothing: if any entry cannot be read while the
directory is being listed, an error is returned instead of a partial list.

items.name: utf8
items.docs:
Create a UTF-8 path from a dynamic `Str`. String literals can be used
directly wherever a `Path` is expected.

items.name: from_quote
items.docs: Create a UTF-8 text path from a quoted literal.

items.name: from_interpolation
items.docs:
Create a UTF-8 path from an interpolated string literal.
This performs textual concatenation; use [join] for path-component joining.

items.name: parser_for
items.docs: Parse and encode every path representation as a lossless tagged value.

items.name: unix
items.docs: Create a Unix path from a Roc string by storing its UTF-8 bytes.

items.name: unix_bytes
items.docs: Create a Unix path from raw bytes without validating UTF-8.

items.name: windows
items.docs: Create a Windows path from a Roc string by storing its UTF-16 code units.

items.name: windows_u16s
items.docs: Create a Windows path from raw UTF-16 code units.

items.name: to_str
items.docs: Convert a path to a string if its raw representation is valid text.

items.name: display
items.docs:
Convert a path to a best-effort display string, replacing invalid text with
U+FFFD. This representation is lossy and must not be used for roundtripping.

items.name: to_inspect
items.docs: Render a path for debugging without losing raw OS units.

items.name: is_eq
items.docs:
Compare paths by content, whichever representation holds it.

A string literal is stored as UTF-8, while the operating system hands
back native units, so `Path.list!("src")?.contains("src/main.roc")`
compares text with native units. The rules are those of
[`OsStr.is_eq`](OsStr#is_eq): valid Unicode is equal when it is the same
text, and invalid native units equal only identical units of the same kind.

Paths are not normalized. `a/b` and `a\b`, `./a` and `a`, and names that
differ in case or Unicode normal form are all unequal, even where the
file system would treat them as one file.

items.name: to_hash
items.docs: Hash paths consistently with [is_eq].

items.name: filename
items.docs: Returns everything after the last directory separator.

items.name: ext
items.docs:
Returns everything after the first dot in the filename that is not a
leading dot: `txt` for `notes.txt`, `tar.gz` for `archive.tar.gz`, and
nothing for `.gitignore`.

items.name: join
items.docs: Adds a separator and a string component to the path.

items.name: to_raw
items.docs: Expose the raw OS-specific representation.

items.name: from_raw
items.docs: Build a path from the raw OS-specific representation.

items.name: seed_u64!
items.docs: Generate a random 64-bit unsigned integer seed.

items.name: seed_u32!
items.docs: Generate a random 32-bit unsigned integer seed.

items.name: catch!
items.docs:
Add events to those caught for the lifetime of this process.
`Interrupt` catches Ctrl-C. `Terminate(unix)` catches Unix SIGTERM,
including systemd's default stop request. Duplicate registrations and an
empty list do nothing. Repeated events coalesce and never force exit.

items.name: poll!
items.docs:
Acknowledge pending events, returning each kind at most once, in
Interrupt/Terminate order. An interrupted effect does not acknowledge
events itself. Native forced termination cannot be caught.

items.name: millis!
items.docs: Sleep for the specified number of milliseconds.

items.name: seconds!
items.docs:
Sleep for the specified number of seconds.

The duration is truncated to whole milliseconds, so `Sleep.seconds!(1.5)`
sleeps for 1500 ms. Negative and `NaN` durations return immediately, and
durations too long for the host to count saturate at about 584 years.

items.name: Value
items.docs: A value bound to a parameter or read from a column.
items.head: Value

items.name: OpenOptions
items.docs:
How to open a database; `{}` takes every default.

`mode` is `ReadWriteCreate` (create the file if it is missing),
`ReadWrite` (the file must exist) or `ReadOnly` (the file must exist and
every write fails with `Failed({ code: ReadOnly, .. })`).

`busy_timeout` is how long a statement waits for another connection's
lock before failing with `Failed({ code: Busy, .. })`. `Duration.zero`
fails at once.
items.head: OpenOptions

items.name: open!
items.docs:
Open a connection to the database file at `path`.

Every call opens a new connection, also for a path that is already
open. The path `":memory:"` opens a new, private in-memory database,
like [open_in_memory!].

```roc
db = Sqlite.open!("app.db", {})?
readonly = Sqlite.open!("app.db", { mode: ReadOnly })?
```

items.name: open_in_memory!
items.docs:
Open a new, private in-memory database. It is discarded when the
connection is closed or released.

items.name: Db
items.docs:
A connection to one database.

The connection is closed when the last reference to the `Db`, and to
every unfinished [Db.rows] stream made from it, is released. [close!]
closes it earlier and reports a failure to do so.

The connection keeps the statements it has prepared, keyed by their SQL
text, so running the same text again does not prepare it again. It keeps
at most 32, dropping the least recently used.
items.head: Db

items.name: to_inspect
items.docs: Render the connection without exposing its host handle.

items.name: close!
items.docs:
Close the connection now. An open transaction is rolled back, and
every unfinished [Db.rows] stream ends with `Err(Closed)`.

After `close!`, every other method returns `Err(Closed)`. Closing a
closed connection is `Ok({})`.

items.name: execute!
items.docs:
Run one statement that returns no rows, such as an `INSERT`,
`UPDATE`, `DELETE` or `CREATE TABLE`.

A statement with result columns is rejected before it runs with
`ReturnsRows`, even if it would return no row; so an
`INSERT … RETURNING` inserts nothing. Text holding a second
statement is rejected with `MultipleStatements`; use
[execute_script!] for that. Text holding no statement at all, only
white space or comments, does nothing.

```roc
db.execute!("INSERT INTO todos (task) VALUES (${String(task)})")?
```

items.name: execute_script!
items.docs:
Run every statement in `sql`, in order, stopping at the first one
that fails. The statements take no parameters, and any rows they
return are discarded.

The statements are not wrapped in a transaction: those before a
failing one have taken effect, unless the text itself has a `BEGIN`
or the call is made inside [transaction!].

```roc
db.execute_script!(
    \\CREATE TABLE todos (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, task TEXT NOT NULL);
    \\CREATE INDEX todos_task ON todos (task);
)?
```

items.name: query_one!
items.signature: Db, Query, Decoder(a, err) => Try(a, [Interrupted, SqliteErr(Err), Closed, NoRows, TooManyRows, BadRow(err)])
items.docs:
Run a query that returns exactly one row and decode it.

No row is `Err(NoRows)` and a second row is `Err(TooManyRows)`. A row
whose values the decoder rejects is `Err(BadRow(err))`.

```roc
count = db.query_one!("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM todos", Decoder.i64(0))?
```

items.name: query_all!
items.signature: Db, Query, Decoder(a, err) => Try(List(a), [Interrupted, SqliteErr(Err), Closed, BadRow(err)])
items.docs:
Run a query and decode every row into a list.

The first row whose values the decoder rejects ends the query with
`Err(BadRow(err))`; to skip such rows instead, use [Db.rows].

```roc
tasks = db.query_all!("SELECT task FROM todos ORDER BY id", Decoder.str("task"))?
```

items.name: rows
items.signature: Db, Query, Decoder(a, err) -> Stream(Try(a, [Interrupted, SqliteErr(Err), Closed, BadRow(err)]))
items.docs:
Lazily run a query, decoding one row for each item pulled.

Building the stream does nothing; the first pull prepares the
statement, binds its parameters and resolves the decoder's columns.
The stream ends after the last row.

A `BadRow(err)` item concerns one row, whose values the decoder
rejected, and the stream continues with the next row. A `SqliteErr`
or `Closed` item is the last one. A column the decoder names that
the query does not return is `Err(SqliteErr(ColumnNotFound(_)))`,
the only item.

```roc
for! item in db.rows("SELECT id, payload FROM events ORDER BY id", decode_event) {
    match item {
        Ok(event) if event.id > last => break
        Ok(event) => Stdout.line!(event.payload)?
        Err(BadRow(_)) => {}
        Err(SqliteErr(err)) => { return Err(SqliteErr(err)) }
        Err(Interrupted) => { return Err(Interrupted) }
        Err(Closed) => { return Err(Closed) }
    }
}
```

The stream holds its statement, and with it SQLite's read lock, until
it has finished or is released. The connection stays usable
meanwhile, also for another stream of the same query.

A stream left with `break` is released when the function containing
the loop returns, not at the end of the loop
([roc-lang/roc#12266](https://github.com/roc-lang/roc/issues/12266)).
Give the loop a function of its own if the lock has to be gone before
the next statement, such as a `DROP TABLE`.

items.name: transaction!
items.signature: Db, (() => Try(a, [Interrupted, SqliteErr(Err), Closed, ..errs])) => Try(a, [Interrupted, SqliteErr(Err), Closed, ..errs])

items.name: Query
items.docs:
SQL text and the values of its parameters.

A string literal is a `Query`. Each `${…}` in it must be a [Value] and
becomes a bound parameter (`?1`, `?2`, …), so the value is never parsed
as SQL:

```roc
db.execute!("UPDATE todos SET status = ${String(status)} WHERE id = ${Integer(id)}")?
```

A `${…}` inside `'…'`, `"…"` or a comment would be text, not a
parameter, so such a literal is rejected at compile time; write
`name = ${String(name)}`, not `name = '${String(name)}'`.
items.head: Query

items.name: from_quote
items.docs: A string literal without interpolation: SQL with no parameters.

items.name: from_interpolation
items.docs: An interpolated string literal: each `${…}` is a bound parameter.

items.name: new
items.docs:
SQL assembled at run time, with the values for its `?` markers in
order. A count that differs from the statement's number of
parameters is `WrongParamCount` when the query is run.

```roc
marks = Str.join_with(ids.map(|_| "?"), ", ")
query = Query.new("SELECT task FROM todos WHERE id IN (${marks})", ids.map(|id| Integer(id)))
```

items.name: Column
items.docs:
A result column, by name or by position counted from zero. A string
literal is a name and a number literal is a position:
`Decoder.i64("id")`, `Decoder.i64(0)`.

A name must match the column's name in the result exactly; give an
expression a name with `AS`. Where two columns have the same name, the
name selects the first.

[
		Error,
		Internal,
		Perm,
		Abort,
		Busy,
		Locked,
		NoMem,
		ReadOnly,

items.docs:
SQLite's primary result codes for a failure. A constraint violation
says which kind of constraint failed.
items.head: ErrCode

items.name: Err
items.signature:
[
		Failed({ code : ErrCode, extended_code : I64, message : Str }),
		ColumnNotFound(Column),
		WrongParamCount({ expected : U64, given : U64 }),
		ReturnsRows,
		MultipleStatements,
	]
items.docs:
Why a database call failed.

`Failed` is an error reported by SQLite: its primary result code, its
[extended result code](https://www.sqlite.org/rescode.html) and its
message. The other variants mean the call does not fit the statement,
and are found before anything runs:

- `ColumnNotFound`: a decoder reads a column the query does not return.
- `WrongParamCount`: the statement has `expected` parameters and the
  [Query] carries `given` values.
- `ReturnsRows`: a statement given to [Db.execute!] has result columns.
- `MultipleStatements`: the text holds more than one statement.
items.head: Err

items.name: to_str
items.docs: Describe the error for display.

items.name: DecodeErr
items.signature:
[
		UnexpectedType({ column : Str, found : [Null, Integer, Real, String, Bytes] }),
		BadUtf8({ problem : Str.Utf8Problem, index : U64 }),
	]
items.docs:
What the leaf decoders report: a column holding another type than the
one asked for, or text that is not valid UTF-8.
items.head: DecodeErr

items.name: Row
items.docs: A whole result row, as decoded by [Decoder.row].
items.head: Row

items.name: Decoder
items.docs:
How to turn a result row into an `a`, or fail with an `err`.

Leaf decoders read one column. Records of decoders combine with the
record-builder suffix:

```roc
decode_todo : Decoder({ id : I64, task : Str }, Sqlite.DecodeErr)
decode_todo = { id: Decoder.i64("id"), task: Decoder.str("task") }.Decoder
```

A decoder's columns are looked up once per query, before its first row
is read; a column that is missing is `SqliteErr(ColumnNotFound(_))`.
A value the decoder rejects fails that row only, as `BadRow(err)`.

SQLite stores a value with its own type, whatever the column was
declared as, and the leaf decoders do not convert: `i64` accepts only
an integer.
items.head: Decoder(a, err)

items.name: map2
items.signature: Decoder(a, err), Decoder(b, err), (a, b -> c) -> Decoder(c, err)
items.docs:
Combine two decoders; this is what the record-builder suffix
`{ … }.Decoder` calls.

items.name: map
items.docs: Transform the decoded value.

items.name: map_try
items.signature: Decoder(a, err), (a -> Try(b, err)) -> Decoder(b, err)
items.docs:
Transform the decoded value with a function that can fail; its
error fails the row, beside the decoder's own errors.

```roc
Decoder.i64("age").map_try(|n| if n >= 0 { Ok(n) } else { Err(NegativeAge(n)) })
```

decoder reads is `NULL`, and `Ok` of the decoded value otherwise.

items.name: line!
items.docs:
Write the given string to [standard error](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_streams#Standard_error_(stderr)),
followed by a newline.

> To write to `stderr` without the newline, see [Stderr.write!].

items.name: write!
items.docs:
Write the given string to [standard error](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_streams#Standard_error_(stderr)).

Most terminals will not actually display strings that are written to them until they receive a newline,
so this may appear to do nothing until you write a newline!

> To write to `stderr` with a newline at the end, see [Stderr.line!].

items.name: write_bytes!
items.docs:
Write the given bytes to [standard error](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_streams#Standard_error_(stderr)).

Most terminals will not actually display content that are written to them until they receive a newline,
so this may appear to do nothing until you write a newline!

items.name: line!
items.signature: () => Try(Str, [EndOfInput, Interrupted, BadUtf8({ problem : Str.Utf8Problem, index : U64 }), StdinErr(IOErr)])
items.docs:
Read a line from [standard input](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_streams#Standard_input_(stdin)).

A line ends at `\n`. The terminator is not returned, and one `\r` before
it is removed. Input that ends without a `\n` still yields its last
line; after that the result is `Err(EndOfInput)`. An empty line is
`Ok("")`.

A line that is not valid UTF-8 is consumed and reported as `BadUtf8`;
the next call reads the line after it.

> This function will block the program from continuing until `stdin` receives a newline character
(e.g. because the user pressed Enter in the terminal), so using it can result in the appearance of the
program having gotten stuck. It's often helpful to print a prompt first, so
the user knows it's necessary to enter something before the program will continue.

items.name: bytes!
items.docs:
Read bytes from [standard input](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_streams#Standard_input_(stdin)).

Returns at least one byte and no more than 16,384, or `Err(EndOfInput)`
once the input has ended. Use [chunks] to process all of the input a
piece at a time, or [read_to_end!] to collect it.

> This is typically used in combination with [Tty.enable_raw_mode!],
which disables default terminal behaviour and allows reading input
without buffering until Enter key is pressed.

items.name: read_to_end!
items.docs:
Read all bytes from [standard input](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_streams#Standard_input_(stdin))
until [EOF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End-of-file) in this source.

items.name: lines
items.signature: () -> Stream(Try(Str, [Interrupted, BadUtf8({ problem : Str.Utf8Problem, index : U64 }), StdinErr(IOErr)]))

items.name: chunks
items.docs:
Lazily read standard input as non-empty chunks of bytes, as [bytes!]
does. Chunk boundaries do not correspond to lines or text encoding
boundaries.

Building the stream reads nothing. The stream ends at the end of input,
and a `StdinErr` item is the last one. Each item is one read and the
stream holds no input of its own, so it can follow [line!] or [lines]
without losing a byte.

```roc
for! item in Stdin.chunks() {
    Stdout.write_bytes!(item?)?
}
```

Write the given string to [standard output](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_streams#Standard_output_(stdout)),
followed by a newline.

> To write to `stdout` without the newline, see [Stdout.write!].

so this may appear to do nothing until you write a newline!

items.name: Listener
items.docs:
A listening socket.

The socket is closed when the last reference to the listener is
released, or earlier by [close!]. Copies of a listener share one
socket, so closing one closes them all.

items.docs:
The port this listener is bound to. After `Tcp.listen!(host, 0, …)`
this is the port the operating system chose. `Closed` after [close!].

items.docs:
Stop listening and release the port. Closing again succeeds.
Connections already accepted stay open.

items.name: listen!
items.docs:
Bind an address and listen for connections. Port zero asks the operating
system for a free port, which [Listener.local_port!] reports. The
timeout covers hostname resolution.

```roc
listener = Tcp.listen!("127.0.0.1", 0, Duration.seconds(5))?
port = listener.local_port!()?
```

items.signature: { host : Resource.TcpConnection, timeout : Duration, line_limit : U64 }
items.docs:
A buffered TCP connection, with the I/O timeout and line limit its
reads and writes use.

The connection is closed when the last reference to it is released.
Copies of a connection share one socket and one buffer, so every read,
whether of lines, delimited bytes or binary data, continues where the
previous one stopped. [Connection.with_timeout] and
[Connection.with_line_limit] change the settings of the copy they return,
not the socket.

Every read ends the same way: once the peer has closed its side and all
data has been returned, the next read is `Err(EndOfInput)`. An empty
`Ok` is real data, such as an empty line.

A read that times out consumes nothing. Bytes that had arrived stay
buffered for the next read, so a client may simply read again. A write
that times out may have sent any prefix of its bytes: drop the
connection unless the protocol can resynchronise.

items.docs: Render the connection without exposing its host handle.

with_line_limit
items.docs:
The same connection with another limit, in bytes, on one record read
by [read_until!], [read_line!] or [Connection.lines]. The delimiter
or line terminator counts towards the limit. The default is
1,048,576 (1 MiB).

items.name: read_up_to!
items.docs:
Read at most `max_bytes` bytes, returning as soon as any have
arrived. Short reads are valid. Asking for zero bytes returns
`Ok([])` without waiting; otherwise the result is never empty, and a
closed peer is `Err(EndOfInput)`.

items.name: read_exactly!
items.docs:
Read exactly `count` bytes. Zero succeeds without waiting.

If the peer closes before `count` bytes arrive the result is
`Err(UnexpectedEndOfInput)`. The bytes that did arrive are not
consumed: [read_up_to!] returns them.

items.name: read_until!
items.signature: Connection, U8 => Try(List(U8), [EndOfInput, Interrupted, ReadLimitExceeded(U64), TcpErr(IOErr)])
items.docs:
Read bytes through and including the next `delimiter`.

If the peer closes first, the bytes before the end are returned
without a delimiter, and the read after that is `Err(EndOfInput)`.
So the result is never empty, and its last byte shows whether the
delimiter arrived.

A record longer than the connection's line limit is
`Err(ReadLimitExceeded(limit))`. The rest of that record, through
its delimiter, is then discarded before the next read returns, as
part of that read and within its timeout.

```roc
field = conn.read_until!('|')?
```

items.name: read_line!
items.signature: Connection => Try(Str, [EndOfInput, ReadLimitExceeded(U64), BadUtf8({ problem : Str.Utf8Problem, index : U64 }), Interrupted, TcpErr(IOErr)])
items.docs:
Read a line of text.

A line ends at `\n`. The terminator is not returned, and one `\r`
before it is removed. If the peer closes without a final `\n` the
last line is still returned; after that the result is
`Err(EndOfInput)`. An empty line is `Ok("")`.

A line longer than the connection's line limit is
`Err(ReadLimitExceeded(limit))`, and a line that is not valid UTF-8
is `BadUtf8`. Either way that line is skipped and the next call
reads the line after it. For the bytes of a line, use
`conn.read_until!('\n')`.

items.name: write_bytes!
items.docs: Write all of `bytes`. They are sent at once, not buffered.

items.name: write_utf8!
items.docs: Write a string as UTF-8. It is sent at once, not buffered.

items.name: chunks
items.docs:
Lazily read this connection as non-empty chunks of at most 64 KiB,
each returned as soon as it arrives. Chunk boundaries do not
correspond to the peer's writes, records, or text encoding
boundaries. For a chosen size, call [read_up_to!] in a loop.

Building the stream reads nothing; each item is one read with the
connection's timeout. The stream ends when the peer closes. A
`TcpErr` item, including `TcpErr(TimedOut)`, is the last one; the
connection stays usable and a new stream may be started.

```roc
for! item in conn.chunks() {
    bytes = item?
    $total = $total + bytes.len()
}
```

The stream holds no data of its own, so it can be mixed with the
other reads and with writes. It keeps the connection open until it
has finished or is released.

items.name: connect!
items.signature: Str, U16, { connect_timeout : Duration, io_timeout : Duration } => Try(Connection, [Interrupted, TcpErr(IOErr)])
items.docs:
Open a TCP connection.

`connect_timeout` bounds this call, across hostname resolution and every
address the name resolves to. `io_timeout` is the timeout the new
[Connection] holds for its reads and writes.

A port nobody listens on is `Err(TcpErr(ConnectionRefused))` once the
operating system reports it. Windows retries for about two seconds
first, so a shorter `connect_timeout` gives `Err(TcpErr(TimedOut))` there.

```roc
conn = Tcp.connect!("localhost", 8080, { connect_timeout: Duration.seconds(1), io_timeout: Duration.seconds(5) })?
```

Valid hostnames look like `127.0.0.1`, `::1`, `localhost`, or `roc-lang.org`.

items.name: enable_raw_mode!
items.docs:
Enable terminal [raw mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminal_mode) to disable some default terminal behaviour.

This leads to the following changes:
- Input will not be echoed to the terminal screen.
- Input will be sent straight to the program instead of being buffered (= collected) until the Enter key is pressed.
- Special keys like Backspace and CTRL+C will not be processed by the terminal driver but will be passed to the program.

Calling this when raw mode is already enabled does nothing and returns `Ok`.
Calls are not counted, so a single [Tty.disable_raw_mode!] undoes any number
of calls to this function.

Returns a `TtyErr` when the process has no terminal to configure (for
example when it runs detached from a terminal), or when the operating
system rejects the change. The terminal mode is left untouched in that case.

items.name: disable_raw_mode!
items.docs:
Revert the terminal to the mode it was in before [Tty.enable_raw_mode!] was called.

Calling this when raw mode is not enabled does nothing and returns `Ok`;
the platform only ever reverts a mode that it enabled itself.

Returns a `TtyErr` when the operating system rejects the change. Raw mode
is still considered enabled in that case, so this can be called again and
the platform will retry when the app finishes.

items.name: Url
items.signature:
{
	scheme : [Http, Https],
	host : Str,
	port : [None, Some(U16)],
	path : Str,
	query : [None, Some(Str)],
	fragment : [None, Some(Str)],
}
items.docs:
A validated HTTP or HTTPS URL implemented entirely in Roc.

This is deliberately stricter than a browser parser. Hosts must be ASCII
DNS names, dotted-decimal IPv4 addresses, or bracketed IPv6 addresses made
from hexadecimal groups with optional :: elision. IPv4-in-IPv6 and Unicode
domain names are intentionally unsupported.

items.signature:
[
		CredentialsNotAllowed,
		EmptyHost,
		InternationalHostUnsupported,
		InvalidCharacter(U8),
		InvalidHost(Str),
		InvalidIpv4(Str),
		InvalidIpv6(Str),
		InvalidPercentEncoding(U64),
		InvalidPort(Str),
		MissingAuthority,
		MissingScheme,
		PortOutOfRange(U64),

items.docs:
A reason a URL or relative reference could not be parsed.

This error set describes this module's strict HTTP/HTTPS subset. Inputs
that browsers might repair, such as missing authority slashes or
backslashes, are rejected instead.

items.name: parse
items.docs:
Parse a dynamic string as an absolute HTTP or HTTPS URL.

The input must contain an explicit scheme and authority. Its host is
lowercased, default ports are removed, dot path segments are normalized,
and non-ASCII path, query, and fragment bytes are percent-encoded.

items.name: from_quote
items.docs:
Convert a quoted literal to a URL using the same validation as parse.

Roc calls this automatically when a quoted literal is expected to have
type Url. A rejected literal reports a descriptive BadQuotedBytes error.

		where [
			encoding.parse_str : encoding, state -> Try({ value : Str, rest : state }, err),
			encoding.invalid_value : encoding, state -> err,

items.name: to_str
items.docs:
Serialize the URL in a stable normalized ASCII form.

Scheme and DNS host names are lowercase, default ports are omitted,
paths are absolute, and IPv6 addresses use eight unpadded groups.

items.name: to_inspect
items.docs: Render a URL for debugging and test failures.

items.name: is_eq
items.docs: Compare URLs by their canonical serialized representation.

items.name: to_hash
items.docs: Hash URLs consistently with canonical equality.

items.name: scheme
items.docs: Return Http or Https.

items.name: host
items.docs:
Return the canonical host.

IPv6 brackets are omitted; to_str includes them where required.

items.name: port
items.docs:
Return an explicit non-default port.

Ports 80 for HTTP and 443 for HTTPS are canonicalized to None.

items.name: path
items.docs: Return the absolute percent-encoded path, always beginning with slash.

items.name: query
items.docs:
Return the percent-encoded query without its leading question mark.

None and Some("") distinguish no query from a present empty query.

items.name: fragment
items.docs:
Return the percent-encoded fragment without its leading hash.

None and Some("") distinguish no fragment from a present empty fragment.

items.name: without_fragment
items.docs: Return this URL without its fragment. HTTP never transmits fragments.

items.name: resolve
items.docs:
Resolve a strict relative reference or absolute web URL against this URL.

Root-relative, path-relative, query-only, and fragment-only references
are supported. Scheme-relative references are rejected.

items.name: append_path_segments
items.docs:
Append unencoded path segments.

Each list item is one segment, so slash characters inside an item are
percent-encoded rather than treated as separators.

items.name: append_query_param
items.docs:
Append one application/x-www-form-urlencoded query pair.

Existing parameters, ordering, duplicate names, and the fragment are
preserved.

items.name: query_pairs
items.docs:
Decode the query into ordered name/value pairs.

Plus signs decode as spaces, percent escapes decode as UTF-8 bytes,
parameters without equals receive an empty value, and duplicates remain.

items.name: with_query
items.docs:
Replace or remove the query.

Some("") produces a present empty query. The supplied query may contain
Unicode but must otherwise already obey URL query syntax.

items.name: with_fragment
items.docs:
Replace or remove the fragment.

Some("") produces a present empty fragment. Unicode is percent-encoded.

items.name: Utc
items.docs:
A point in calendar time: signed nanoseconds since the Unix epoch,
1970-01-01T00:00:00Z. Instants before 1970 are negative.

`Utc` values support `==` and the ordering operators and sort with
`List.sort`. The time between two of them is a [Duration], from
[Utc.since]. To measure how long something took, prefer [Monotonic], which
is unaffected by changes to the wall clock.

This platform supplies clock effects and signed epoch conversions. Use a
package such as [roc-time](https://github.com/lukewilliamboswell/roc-time)
for timestamp parsing, calendar operations and richer formatting. Its
[supported profiles](https://lukewilliamboswell.github.io/roc-time/profiles.html#profiles)
describe the accepted formats and precision; roc-time 0.3 uses microseconds,
while `Utc` stores nanoseconds. Convert units explicitly at that boundary.
[Utc.to_iso_8601] is a convenience display at whole-second precision.
Use [Utc.to_nanos_since_epoch] and [Utc.from_nanos_since_epoch] for exact
timestamp storage. Parsing and richer formatting are outside this module's
scope rather than planned additions to the native host.

Every result is clamped to what its type holds, so nothing here crashes on
overflow: a `Utc` to the [I128] range, a [Duration] to zero and its maximum.
items.head: Utc

items.name: now!
items.docs:
Read the current time from the system clock.

A clock set before 1970 gives a negative instant rather than an error or
the epoch.

items.name: from_nanos_since_epoch
items.docs:
The instant a number of nanoseconds after the Unix epoch, or before it
when negative.

items.name: to_nanos_since_epoch
items.docs: Nanoseconds from the Unix epoch to this instant, negative before 1970.

items.name: from_millis_since_epoch
items.docs:
The instant a number of milliseconds after the Unix epoch, or before it
when negative, clamped to the representable range.

items.name: to_millis_since_epoch
items.docs:
Whole milliseconds from the Unix epoch to this instant, negative before
1970. A partial millisecond is floored, so one nanosecond before the epoch
is millisecond -1.

items.name: since
items.docs:
The time from an earlier instant to this one: `later.since(earlier)`.

The arguments are directional. When `earlier` is in fact the later
instant the result is [Duration.zero], and a span too long for a
[Duration] is clamped to the longest one.

```roc
stale = Utc.now!().since(path.time_modified!()?) > Duration.minutes(5)
```

items.name: to_iso_8601
items.docs:
Format this instant as an ISO 8601 UTC string with second precision,
flooring any partial second: `2026-10-13T09:30:00Z`.

The stored nanoseconds are unchanged, but this string omits them; use
[to_nanos_since_epoch] when the full precision must round-trip. There
is no corresponding parser here; use a time package for text interchange.

Instants before 1970 are formatted too, in the proleptic Gregorian
calendar. Years outside 0000 to 9999 use the expanded form with a sign,
such as `-0001-12-31T23:59:59Z`.

items.name: to_inspect
items.docs: How `Str.inspect` renders an instant: `Utc(2026-10-13T09:30:00Z)`.

items.name: is_eq
items.docs: Compare two instants for equality (`==` and `!=`).

items.name: is_lt
items.docs: Whether the first instant is earlier than the second (`<`).

items.name: is_lte
items.docs: Whether the first instant is no later than the second (`<=`).

items.name: is_gt
items.docs: Whether the first instant is later than the second (`>`).

items.name: is_gte
items.docs: Whether the first instant is no earlier than the second (`>=`).

items.name: order_relative_to
items.docs:
Order two instants, earliest first. This is what `List.sort` and
`List.sort_by` use.
